planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Superspur was selected for its heavily spurred fruiting wood, which sets an unusually dense crop, and benefits from a second mayhaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a wetland native that tolerates the poorly drained, low-lying ground where most other fruit trees decline. Superspur is a named western mayhaw selection valued by Gulf South growers for the unusually dense, short fruiting spurs that line its branches, packing on a heavier crop of small, tart, aromatic red berries than many seedling or older cultivars produce. Fruit ripens in May, giving the tree its common name, and is harvested from the ground or by shaking branches over tarps for the classic mayhaw jelly of Louisiana, Mississippi, and east Texas. Plant with a second mayhaw cultivar for best cross-pollination and yield, and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years and to keep improving in production for decades.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Mayhaw Production and Culture
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Mayhaw for Gulf Coast

common_name: Texas Star Mayhaw (Large-Fruited Western Mayhaw Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Texas Star was selected for its above-average fruit size among western mayhaws and produces best with a second mayhaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil where the tree's native wetland preference lets it thrive on low, poorly drained ground unsuitable for most other fruit trees. Texas Star is a named western mayhaw selection prized among east Texas and Gulf South growers for fruit that runs noticeably larger than wild-collected mayhaw, borne in heavy clusters of bright red, tart, aromatic berries that ripen in May. The larger fruit size makes hand harvest more efficient for home jelly-making, one of the enduring regional food traditions of the Gulf South. Plant alongside a second mayhaw cultivar for best cross-pollination, and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years, becoming increasingly productive as it matures.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Mayhaw for Gulf Coast
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Mayhaw Production and Culture

common_name: Prok American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Cold-Hardy Native Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Prok is a self-fertile American persimmon selection that sets seedless fruit without a pollinator, though it tolerates a very wide range of soils and some drought once established.

directions: Plant a bare-root or container-grown tree in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; American persimmon develops a long taproot, so set young trees carefully and avoid transplanting older ones. Prok is a well-known named selection of the native American persimmon valued for its unusually large fruit for the species, along with reliable, heavy, self-fertile production that does not require a second tree for pollination. Orange fruit ripens in fall and is intensely sweet and rich once fully soft-ripe, but astringent and unpalatable if eaten before that point, so wait until fruit is soft to the touch or has dropped naturally. The tree tolerates heat, drought, and a wide range of soils once established, needing little care beyond occasional watering during establishment and removal of root suckers that can form a thicket if left unchecked.
sources: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension — American Persimmon

common_name: Early Golden American Persimmon (Classic Early-Ripening Native Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Early Golden is one of the oldest named American persimmon cultivars, ripening earlier than most and producing well as a single tree, though yields can improve with a second cultivar nearby.

directions: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, siting the tree carefully since American persimmon forms a deep taproot and resents being moved once established. Early Golden is one of the oldest and most widely planted named selections of native American persimmon, valued for ripening earlier in the fall than most other cultivars and for its rich, honey-sweet flavor once fruit is fully soft-ripe. It has served as an important parent in later persimmon breeding programs and remains a dependable choice for home orchards across its hardiness range. Never eat the golden-orange fruit while still firm, since unripe American persimmon is strongly astringent; wait until it softens fully or falls from the tree. The tree tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, and needs little maintenance beyond removing root suckers each year.
sources: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension — American Persimmon

common_name: Meader American Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Self-Fertile Native Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Meader is self-fertile and sets seedless fruit without a second tree, and it was selected in New Hampshire for cold hardiness well beyond the species' typical southern range.

directions: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, taking care with the taproot since American persimmon does not transplant well once established. Meader was selected in New Hampshire and is notable for extending American persimmon culture well north of its typical native range, combining reliable cold hardiness with self-fertile, seedless fruit that a single tree can produce without a pollinator. The medium orange fruit ripens in fall and, like all American persimmon, must soften fully before eating or it will be unpleasantly astringent. It also grows vigorously and fruits reliably in the milder, longer growing seasons of the Gulf South, tolerating heat and a range of soils once established. Water during the first two seasons to establish the taproot, then expect the tree to need little care beyond removing root suckers.
sources: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension — American Persimmon
